posts.title: What a Duplicate Inspection Teaches
posts.excerpt: In aviation maintenance, a duplicate inspection is not a sign of doubt, but a disciplined operational barrier against error that every technician must master.
posts.content:
At 15:00 on any weekday at Tsubasa College, the atmosphere in Hangar 1 and Hangar 2 shifts from the steady clatter of pneumatic tools to deliberate, quiet concentration. The scheduled work on the airframes has concluded for the day, but the maintenance cycle is far from complete. This final working hour before the hangar doors close at 16:00 is reserved for duplicate inspections, maintenance logbook entries, and strict tool control. For students enrolled in our eighteen-month licence-track programme, this afternoon ritual is where technical knowledge transforms into licensed responsibility.

A duplicate inspection is mandatory whenever work disturbs vital aircraft systems whose failure would jeopardize safe flight, including flight control cable runs, engine throttle linkages, and critical locking hardware. The regulatory requirement is deceptively simple: after the technician who performed the task completes and inspects the assembly, an independent, authorized person must conduct a completely separate inspection of the work. Neither person assumes the other was thorough; both inspect every split pin, castellated nut, safety wire twist, and turnbuckle as if their own certification alone confirmed airworthiness.

Under the guidance of Pieter de Vries, who leads our human factors and civil aviation regulation modules, students quickly learn that duplicate inspections are psychological exercises as much as mechanical checks. Confirmation bias is a persistent human vulnerability. When a technician has spent three hours assembling a torque tube or tensioning an aileron control cable, their brain naturally expects every fastener to be secure. The independent inspector must approach the identical mechanism with deliberate detachment, asking not whether the work looks acceptable, but what subtle error might have been overlooked.

In the training hangar, an instructor like Daniel Okafor or Tomás Rivera steps in as the countersigning inspector only after the student has conducted their own preliminary check. Holding a blank checklist card, the instructor watches the student explain the procedure step by step. Which maintenance manual revision governed the task? What torque setting was specified, and which calibrated wrench was checked out from the tool store? Did the cable tension correspond with the ambient hangar temperature chart? The student must physically verify every lockwire and cotter pin in the presence of the countersigner.

This discipline reinforces the founding principle established by Henrik Aalto when Tsubasa College first opened its doors in 1998: we teach on real aircraft, and every task is signed and countersigned. There is no partial credit in maintenance record-keeping. If a task card is signed before the work is verified, or if a duplicate inspection is treated as a perfunctory formality, the exercise is halted immediately for a thorough case debrief.

When the second signature is applied to the task card, it signifies more than technical compliance. It represents mutual trust between two professionals who have examined the same mechanical assembly from independent perspectives. As toolboxes are locked and shadow boards counted down to the last socket at 16:00, students understand that a duplicate inspection does not signify lack of confidence. Instead, it is the highest expression of professional humility and the foundational safeguard of civil aviation safety.

posts.title: Reading a borescope image
posts.excerpt: Interpreting discoloration and wear on a turbine blade through a borescope, and why the first skill is steady hands, not a trained eye.
posts.content:
A borescope lets a technician look inside an engine without taking it apart. The picture on the small screen is flat, bright at the centre and dark at the edges, and everything in it looks about the same size until you learn what to compare it with. In the powerplant module we start with a reference blade on a bench, so that students know what normal looks like before they meet something that is not.

The skill that takes longest is not interpretation but control. The probe has to be guided through a narrow port, rotated, articulated and held still while the image settles. Students practise on a cutaway engine until they can bring the tip to a chosen blade edge without hunting for it, and only then do they move to a real engine in Hangar 2.

Every inspection ends with a written note: what was seen, where, and what was decided. A discoloured blade tip may be harmless or may be the first sign of a hot section problem, and the note, countersigned by the instructor, is what the next technician will rely on.

posts.title: A first week in Hangar 2
posts.excerpt: How new students move from classroom fundamentals to live airframes in their first five days at Carrow Field.
posts.content:
The first Monday starts at 07:30 with tool control. Each student receives a toolbox, counts every item against the shadow board and signs for it. It takes forty minutes, and by Friday nobody needs reminding why it matters: a missing wrench inside an airframe is a finding, not an inconvenience.

On Tuesday and Wednesday the cohort splits into groups of six and rotates between the workshop, where they practise measuring, filing and drilling on scrap, and the hangar, where they watch second-year students work a task card on a real aircraft. They are not allowed to touch yet, but they are allowed to ask anything.

By Friday afternoon each student has signed their first task card, a simple panel removal and refit with an instructor at their side. The hangar closes at 16:00, the tools are counted again and the week ends with a short debrief on what went well and what did not.
